Cyberattack Disrupts Libya’s Payments and Telecommunications Systems, Hampering Economy

TRIPOLI, June 25—A widespread cyberattack on Libya’s national payments and telecommunications networks is disrupting economic activity across the country, officials and business groups said Tuesday, as authorities struggled to contain the ongoing incident.

The attack began late Monday, targeting electronic payment processors and major telecom exchanges in Tripoli and Benghazi, according to the National Cybersecurity Authority. By midday Tuesday, electronic transactions at most banks and retail outlets had halted, and intermittent outages were reported in mobile and internet services in several cities.

“The systems are under sustained attack. Our teams are working to isolate affected nodes and restore connectivity, but the situation remains fluid,” said Kareem al-Bouri, spokesperson for the National Cybersecurity Authority. He declined to identify the attackers but described the incident as “coordinated and sophisticated.”

The disruptions have left many Libyans unable to withdraw cash, pay bills, or access online services. Small businesses in Tripoli’s central market reported a sharp drop in trade, as most customers use digital payments to complete transactions.

“We rely on the electronic system for almost everything—salaries, supplies, even simple sales,” said Fatima Elmasri, who manages a grocery store in Tripoli. “Today, we had to turn customers away.”

The Libyan Chamber of Commerce estimated that retail trade volumes in the capital fell by at least 60% compared to last week. Factories in Misrata and Benghazi reported delays in payroll and supply chain operations due to the payment system outage.

“We have trucks waiting at the port, but we cannot clear goods without the payment system,” said Ibrahim Dabbashi, head of logistics at the Libyan Maritime Union.

The telecommunications blackout, which affected both the state-run LibTel and private operator SaharaNet, also hampered coordination among emergency services and disrupted business communications nationwide.

Authorities urged the public to remain calm and avoid sharing personal information online. “Our priority is to restore essential services and protect citizens’ data,” al-Bouri said.

Analysts warned that if the disruption persists, it could further strain Libya’s fragile economy. “This highlights the vulnerability of Libya’s infrastructure to cyber threats,” said Samira Jibril, a Tripoli-based cybersecurity expert. “The economic impact could be severe if services are not restored quickly.”
